bai.moTa: Even an object at rest traces a line through spacetime
bai.yChinh: Each object is not a point moving through space, but a **line** in spacetime: its world line. At rest it is a vertical line, at constant velocity a tilted line, and in circular motion a helix. At true scale, Earth’s world line is almost completely straight.
bai.conSo.1: **299,792.458 km**: the length corresponding to one second on the time axis.
bai.conSo.2: **A factor of 63,241**: the pitch of Earth’s helix (one light-year) compared with its orbital radius (1 AU).
bai.conSo.3: **0.0057°**: the actual tilt of Earth’s world line relative to the time axis.
bai.conSo.4: **499 seconds**: the time light takes to travel from the Sun to Earth.
bai.hieuDung: **A spacetime diagram is not a photograph.** Nobody stands “outside” spacetime to see the whole block like that. It is a map: each point represents an event. To make it possible to draw, the model here omits one spatial dimension; the actual block has four dimensions.
bai.nguon: Planetary positions: NASA/JPL table “Approximate Positions of the Planets” (Standish and Williams), as in Lesson 1. Constants: CODATA 2018, IAU 2012.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: Explain what an event is and why four numbers are needed to specify it.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Read a spacetime diagram: identify the time axis and what a “now” slice represents.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Recognize the world lines of an object at rest, an object moving at constant velocity, an object in circular motion, and a light ray.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Explain why, at true scale, Earth’s world line is nearly straight.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
When you arrange to meet someone, you have to specify two things: **where** and **when**. Leave either one out and you miss each other. Physics calls such a “place + moment” pair an {{sự kiện|event}}: a firecracker popping, two spacecraft meeting, a doorbell ringing.

A place takes three numbers (length, width, height). A moment takes one number. So each event takes **four numbers** $(t;\ x;\ y;\ z)$. The set of all events forms a four-dimensional whole called {{không-thời gian|spacetime}}.

> [Lưu ý] A screen can display only three dimensions. In this model we therefore **omit height** $z$ and use the vertical axis as the **time axis**. The gridded floor represents space (the two dimensions $x$ and $y$). Higher up means later in time.

The green glass pane is **“now”**, rising steadily. Each glowing dot is an event. An event sits fixed inside the block and “happens” only at the moment the pane passes through it.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the green dot at the corner of the pane to move “now” up and down yourself. As it crosses an event, the event flashes and rings a chime; each second mark gives a soft tick. Then switch viewpoints: looking from above, you recover a familiar map and lose all information about “when”; looking from the side, you clearly see which event happens earlier and which happens later.
> [[View from above|tren]] [[Side view|ngang]] [[Oblique view|cheo]]

> [Lưu ý] The ticks simply mark time in the model: when the pane advances automatically, each second in the model lasts 1.25 real seconds.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.de: Drag the “now” pane to the exact moment **the two spacecraft meet**, then release it.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.goiY: Hover over the blue dot labeled “Two spacecraft meet” to read its coordinates: $t = 4{,}5$ seconds, halfway between marks 4 and 5 on the time axis.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Place a **house** in the block. It does not budge in space. Yet time keeps passing, so the house is present at the event “house, at 1 second,” then “house, at 2 seconds,” and so on. Joining all those events gives a vertical line: the house’s {{đường thế giới|world line}}.

> [Định nghĩa] A **world line** is the set of all events in the history of an object. Every object, every person, and every particle has a world line.

The little house sitting on the glass pane is the house “right now.” The glowing tube below the pane is its past; the faint dashed section above is its future.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the “now” pane all the way to the bottom and then up to the top. The house never shifts sideways: it simply slides along its own vertical world line.

You are sitting still reading this line, yet in spacetime you are still “traveling”: moving along the time axis. To compare time with length, we multiply time by the speed of light $c$:

$$ 1\ \text{giây} \times c = 299\,792{,}458\ \text{km} $$

In the model, each square on the floor is **one light-second** wide (nearly 300,000 km), and each mark on the time axis is one second. Both axes share the same ruler.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
Add a **spacecraft** flying in a straight line at constant speed. Every second it shifts by the same distance, so its world line is a **tilted** straight line.

The faster it goes, the closer the line leans toward the floor. Let $\theta$ be the angle between the world line and the time axis:

$$ \tan\theta = \frac{\text{quãng đường}}{c \times \text{thời gian}} = \frac{v}{c} $$

> [Thử ngay] Drag the blue dot on the spacecraft’s world line (or use the **Spacecraft speed** slider below). The small arc at the base marks the angle $\theta$; the dashed yellow line is a light ray, tilted at 45°. At $0{,}5\,c$ the line tilts by 26.6°; at $0{,}9\,c$ it tilts by 42°.
> [[Bring to rest|v0]] [[Fly at 0.5 c|v5]] [[Fly at 0.9 c|v9]]

The faint trace on the floor is the spacecraft’s **path through space**, what we usually call its trajectory. It is merely the shadow that the world line casts onto the floor. The shadow does not tell you whether the spacecraft moves fast or slowly; the world line does.

> [Con số] A passenger airliner flies at 900 km/h, or $v/c \approx 8{,}3 \times 10^{-7}$. Its world line tilts by less than 0.00005°. At all everyday speeds, world lines are practically vertical.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: Adjust the spacecraft’s world line so that it tilts at **35°** to the time axis. At what fraction of the speed of light is the spacecraft flying?
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.goiY: Use $\tan\theta = v/c$: $v/c = \tan 35° \approx 0{,}70$. The data panel shows the current tilt angle.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.ten: Light: exactly 45°, and nothing leans further
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
At $t = 1$ second, the house turns on a lamp. The light ray (yellow) travels one light-second every second, so its world line tilts at **exactly 45°**.

Nothing travels faster than light. In geometric terms, **no world line may tilt beyond 45°** from the time axis. Drag the spacecraft’s speed to its maximum: its world line approaches 45° without ever reaching it.

This 45° limit divides spacetime around every event into a “reachable” region and an “unreachable” region. The next lesson builds this boundary into a {{nón ánh sáng|light cone}}.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the “now” pane: at every moment, the distance from the tip of the light ray to the house (in light-seconds) equals the number of seconds elapsed since the lamp turned on. The data panel displays that distance. A soft chime marks the moment the lamp lights up.
> [[Side view to compare angles|ngang]] [[Spacecraft at 0.95 c|v95]]

+++ Go deeper: why choose units in which light tilts at 45°?
If we measured time in seconds and length in meters, a light ray would tilt at 89.9999998°: nearly horizontal, while everything else stood vertical. Such a diagram would be useless.

In relativity we therefore measure time as $ct$ (light-seconds, light-years), or simply “set $c = 1$.” Speed then becomes a dimensionless number between 0 and 1, and light always tilts at 45°.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Move the “now” pane to the moment when the light ray is **3 light-seconds** from the house, then release it.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: The lamp turns on at $t = 1$ second, and light travels one light-second per second. So you need $t = 1 + 3 = 4$ seconds.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Add an **orbiting station** moving in a circle. In space (its shadow on the floor), it retraces the same closed loop over and over. In spacetime, however, it never returns to the same point: by the time it completes one lap, the time is later. Its world line is a **helix**, like a coil spring rising along the time axis.

- The **radius** of the helix equals the orbital radius $R$.
- The **pitch** of the helix (the spacing between successive turns) equals $c \times$ the period $T$.
- The faster it orbits, the tighter the spring compresses; the slower it orbits, the straighter the spring stretches out.

$$ \frac{\text{bước lò xo}}{\text{chu vi quỹ đạo}} = \frac{cT}{2\pi R} = \frac{c}{v} $$

> [Thử ngay] Drag the pink dot at the base of the helix (or use the **Orbiting station speed** slider) and watch the spring compress and stretch. A gentle tone sounds once per revolution: rapid orbits give frequent tones, slow orbits give widely spaced ones.
> [[Slow orbit at 0.2 c|c2]] [[Fast orbit at 0.9 c|c9]] [[View from above|tren]] [[Oblique view|cheo]]

The Moon orbiting Earth, Earth orbiting the Sun, the Sun orbiting the galactic center: all of them trace helices like this. The next step builds the actual helices of the Solar System.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.de: Adjust the orbiting station’s speed until the helix pitch is **15 light-seconds**.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.goiY: Helix pitch $= cT = 2\pi R\,c/v$ with $R = 1{,}7$ light-seconds. Solving gives $v = 2\pi \times 1{,}7/15 \approx 0{,}71\,c$. The data panel shows the current pitch.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.ten: The real Solar System in spacetime
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Here are the four inner planets, with positions calculated from NASA/JPL orbital tables just as in Lesson 1. The grid marks **today**. Below it lies the past: each planet trails its world line, a helix winding around the vertical world line of the Sun.

- Mercury completes an orbit in 88 days: its helix is the most tightly coiled.
- Earth takes one year per turn.
- Mars takes 687 days: its helix is the most stretched.

The grid stays in place while the world lines drift downward as time advances.

> [Thử ngay] Listen: each time a planet completes an orbit, it sounds a note (higher pitch for inner planets, lower for outer ones). At this compression each second represents 3 months, so Mercury chimes nearly once a second, Earth every 4 seconds, and Mars every 7.5 seconds. Hover over a planet to check its period. When viewing all eight planets, only the four giant planets chime, because the four inner planets orbit too rapidly.

> [Lưu ý] To make the coils visible, the time axis here is **compressed about 57,000 times**. One light-year is 63,241 AU long, whereas Earth’s orbital radius is only 1 AU. Drawn to true scale, each turn of Earth’s helix would be 63,241 times as tall as its radius.

The yellow ray joining the Sun to Earth is the sunlight reaching you right now. It left the Sun 8.3 minutes ago. At this compression 8.3 minutes is tiny, so the ray looks nearly horizontal.

[[See all eight planets|tam]] [[Return to the four inner planets|bon]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.ten: Restoring true scale: Earth travels nearly straight
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Click the button below to gradually release the time axis back to true scale. The helices stretch out further and further until they become **nearly vertical** lines.

[[Restore true scale|that]] [[Compress again|nen]]

At true scale, the past below the “today” plane spans only about half an hour. In half an hour, Earth completes only about 1/18,000 of an orbit. The sunlight ray now tilts at 45° like every light ray: it crosses 1 AU in 499 seconds.

Earth orbits the Sun at 29.8 km/s. That sounds fast, yet

$$ \frac{v}{c} = \frac{29{,}8}{299\,792} \approx 10^{-4} $$

so its world line tilts by just 0.0057° from the time axis.

> [Tóm lại] In spacetime, Earth travels **almost straight**. The circular orbit we picture is only the shadow cast on the floor by a nearly straight line.

This is the first clue toward general relativity. The Sun does not need to “pull” Earth around a circle. It only needs to **curve spacetime ever so slightly**, and Earth simply travels “straight” through that curved spacetime. Part 3 develops this idea.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.thuThach.de: Drag the **Time axis** slider until the sunlight ray makes an angle of **30°** with the “today” plane. By what factor is the time axis still compressed?
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.thuThach.goiY: Compressing the time axis by a factor $n$ shortens the vertical span of the sunlight ray by $n$, so its angle with the “today” plane satisfies $\tan = 1/n$. You need $n = 1/\tan 30° = \sqrt 3 \approx 1{,}7$, near the left end of the slider. The data panel shows the current angle.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.ten: Changing the observer: the whole bundle tilts together
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
So far we have drawn everything from the viewpoint of an observer at rest relative to the Sun. Another observer flying past the Solar System at speed $u$ draws a different diagram: for that observer, the Sun and its entire retinue of planets drift backward at speed $u$.

> [Thử ngay] Drag **Observer’s speed**. The Sun’s world line is no longer vertical, and the whole bundle of helices leans together to one side.
> [[Observer at 10 km/s|u10]] [[Fly at 30 km/s|u30]] [[At rest relative to the Sun|u0]]

Notice two things:

1. **No event changes.** Planets still line up or draw apart at the exact same moments. Only the coordinates assigned to events change. World lines are real; “at rest” and “moving” are just descriptions.
2. The “today” grid **remains horizontal**. That is how Galileo and Newton changed reference frames: everyone shares a single “now.” At speeds small compared with light, this rule is extraordinarily accurate. Lesson 6 shows that at high speeds, the “now” slice itself must tilt.

> [Lưu ý] The Milky Way video that inspired this course, along with Lesson 1, shows that very change of reference frame. Seen from the Galaxy, the Sun drifts at 230 km/s, turning the planets’ **paths through space** into helices. In this lesson, the helices are **world lines**: they are already helices even when viewed from the Sun, because time is what stretches them out.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.9.noiDung:
Let us bring together what we have seen:

- Instead of a three-dimensional stage changing over time, we can view the universe as **a four-dimensional block** containing all events.
- Each object is a **line** (or a ribbon) within that block.
- “The world right now” is **a horizontal slice** across the block. The familiar three-dimensional movie is just a sequence of slices stacked one after another.

[[Review the three types of motion|cb]] [[Review the Solar System|hmt]]

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “An object moves along its world line.” Not quite. A world line does not sit inside time waiting for something to move along it; it **already includes** time. The entire curve lies there in the block. What “moves” in the model is only the “now” glass pane, added to help us picture it.

> [Lịch sử] In 1908 Hermann Minkowski, Einstein’s former mathematics professor, recast relativity as the geometry of four-dimensional spacetime and coined the term “world line.” As he put it in essence, space by itself and time by itself would from then on fade into mere shadows, and only a union of the two would remain an independent reality.

Three questions that the rest of this part will answer:

1. What boundary does light carve out inside the four-dimensional block? (Lesson 5: light cones)
2. How does a fast-moving observer slice “now”? (Lesson 6: Lorentz transformations)
3. What does the “length” of a world line mean? (Lesson 6: proper time)
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.y: Multiply time by $c$ so all four coordinates are measured in units of length.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: $\theta$ is the angle from the time axis. Light: 45°. Objects with mass: always less than 45°.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: For Earth around the Sun this ratio is about 10,000: the helix is stretched nearly straight.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: A stone rests motionless on a table. What is its world line in a spacetime diagram?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.1: A single point, because it is not moving
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.2: A straight line parallel to the time axis
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: The stone stays in the same place while time keeps passing, so it is present at that place at every moment: a straight line along the time axis. A single point in the diagram is an **event**, not an object.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: In a diagram with units where $c = 1$, a straight world line tilts at 30° to the time axis. How fast is the object moving?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: $v/c = \tan 30° \approx 0{,}577$. Note that this is neither $\sin 30°$ (which is 0.5) nor $30/90$.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: Why can no object have a horizontal world line?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.1: Because the diagram would be too wide
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.2: Because the object would occupy many places at the same moment, meaning infinite speed
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.3: Because the object would have to be at rest
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.4: Because the time axis is always vertical
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: A horizontal line has the same time coordinate everywhere: the object would be in many places at once, corresponding to infinite speed. Nature’s actual limit is stricter still: no world line can tilt past 45°.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: The Moon orbits Earth at a radius of 384,400 km, taking 27.3 days per revolution. Roughly how many times larger is the pitch of the Moon’s world-line helix than its orbital radius?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: Helix pitch $= cT = 299\,792\ \text{km/s} \times 27{,}3 \times 86\,400\ \text{s} \approx 7{,}07 \times 10^{11}$ km. Dividing by 384,400 km gives about $1{,}84 \times 10^{6}$. The Moon’s helix is stretched almost completely straight.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: Two observers describe the same spacecraft. The first says it is at rest; the second says it is flying at 10 km/s. Who is right, and what do both observers share?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.dap: Both are right: each is using a valid reference frame. What they share are **the events** and **the world line** connecting them: which station the spacecraft meets, when it switches on its lamp, whether it strikes a meteoroid. Changing reference frames only tilts the whole bundle of world lines, without creating or erasing any event.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: E. F. Taylor and J. A. Wheeler, *Spacetime Physics* (2nd edition, 1992), chapters 1 and 5: events, world lines, and reading spacetime diagrams.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapter 4: spacetime diagrams.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: R. P. Feynman, *The Feynman Lectures on Physics*, Vol. I, chapter 17, “Space-Time.”
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: H. Minkowski, lecture “Raum und Zeit” (“Space and Time”), Cologne, 1908.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: A diagram in which one axis represents time (multiplied by $c$) and the remaining axes represent space. Each point is an event, and each object traces a line.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: The set of events that a given observer regards as happening at the same moment: “the world right now” for that observer.
